title: Aliens
creator: James Cameron
review: The perfect sequel, almost better than Ridley Scott’s masterpiece, only hindered by the heavy-handed sentimentality that signals the motherhood theme too overtly at the end. Most sequel films suck because they try to recapture what made the original great, which in film cannot be done since mimicry is the enemy of innovation. Aliens does not simply rehash Alien, and manages as a stand-alone film rather than just an installation in a franchise by progressing from the stalking tension of the first film to action-packed horror. But while Aliens makes enough thematic and atmospheric changes to distinguish itself, it is also brilliant in its retention and development of the ideas Alien first generated. The motherhood and sexual dynamics are turned up another notch as Ripley makes her symbolic adoption and confronts LV-426’s “queen” and as traditional masculine/feminine roles are subverted through the tough female characters and method of alien reproduction. This is an excellent film that is paced perfectly and brings many more new ideas than the simple addition of the ‘s’ to the title would indicate.

title: Bringing Home the Bait
creator: Live Skull
review: Despite being overwhelmingly overlooked or disliked by critics, this album is one of the best and should be far better remembered than it is. In Bringing Home the Bait, Live Skull maintains the nonstop assault established by their debut EP. Three accomplished singers yell or drone on about mutilation, driven on by a powerful, slow bass. Two guitars blanket each other in a wall of sound that can still be picked apart to appreciate the composite riffs. The drumming, of course, is James Lo, one of my favourite drummers of all time. He rarely settles on one constant rhythm, instead playing with the guitar or vocals as if the drums held lyrics of their own. The lyrics themselves feature direct insults to the listeners (“you left the water running”, “all men are born to be so low”), cries of despair (“violence, or the most conscious crime”), and gory announcements (“arms without bodies and brains… big enough”, “takes out his speculum, cold thrust of steel”). In many ways this album abandons traditional rock concepts by purposefully omitting elements such as chorus or melody. It is still recognizable as rock, considering the rock quartet of bass, guitar, and drums. Instead of sounding totally alien, Bringing Home the Bait perverts and corrupts rock.

title: Cavalcade
creator: Black Midi
review: Like many other innovative albums of the internet age, the music in Cavalcade is less a development of new ideas as it is a unique collage of old ones: there’s bossa nova in the rhythm of “Marlene Dietrich”; the singer is mimicking jazz singing in a few songs; the exultant horns at the end of “Ascending Forth” are reminiscent of post-rock acts. Guitarwork is beautiful, a highlight of the album for me, and I am happy that it is the driving force of the album, supporting the melodies as they come and go, defining all the different styles the band employs. This is a very dense album, but its density is not as well executed as other like records, mostly because of the mixing. The vocals are too loud for the number of instruments fighting for attention, and it causes an ugly wall of sound in a few songs. In a way black midi is finally living up to the spirit of their name, although instead of a massive slew of piano notes, the band is blasting a bunch of different instruments at the same time to a similar effect in songs like “John L.” I’m glad I waited to hear this album first as an mp3, instead of the Youtube stream that preceded the streaming release, which would have been even more compressed and difficult to parse. The more minimal songs definitely sound better, even though they’re not as impressive. As with many other recent albums, the vocals don’t work for me and I think the album would have been better without them. This is in stark opposition to the refreshing weirdness of the singing on the band’s debut, which set the album apart from all its peers. Cavalcade sounds flat to me, and while this is in part due to poor layering of instruments, I have noticed that the actual songwriting is a culprit. The crescendoes don’t work very well, and while the songs are pretty I don’t feel a compelling tension and release that would make the album as magnificent as the instruments give it the potential to be. Like a lot of jazz fusion, there is an emotional component missing. Overall this is a technically impressive album with amazing instrumentation that unfortunately gets a bit muddied.

title: ドライブ・マイ・カー [Drive My Car]
creator: 濱口竜介 [Ryusuke Hamaguchi]
review: This film taught me that one important value of slow films is that the long silences and gradually advancing plot give space for feelings to really develop. Inconsequential scenes give time for contemplation of the plot-relevant scenes that precede them. This film is not the best example of this, it’s just the first where I found myself consciously noticing the effect. This film is really pointlessly slow, there are many empty scenes of ugly highway landscapes with banal music overlaid. I am fine with films being slow, but I do not appreciate filler content that does not even seriously contribute to atmosphere. This movie is quite ugly. Most contemporary films are tragically shot on digital, which makes them all look like the same porous hyperreality that could spring CGI on you at any moment. It is very apparent in this film, the long shots of which invite you to stare at actors’ faces in ugly styleless clarity. Love the dream shared between Kafuku, Oto, and Takatsuki. Invites much interpretation. The sole retribution Kafuku attempts on his wife for her infidelity is in refusing to give her the end of her dream-story. Takatsuki reveals that not only did Kafuku’s attempted payback fail, as Oto shared the same story with Takatsuki and therefore learned its plot, but that Oto did not share the ending with Kafuku at all, instead with Takatsuki in one of their trysts. The dream itself is a neat puzzle. The burglar is clearly Kafuku (damage to the left eye), but who are the girl and her prospective beau? I think the uncharacterised boy is also Kafuku, having seen the results of the iniquity performed in his own bed, but pretending that it never happened. If the girl is Oto herself, does she know that Kafuku has seen this infidelity? The girl confesses to the camera, and it is implied that Oto intended to do the same to Kafuku the night she died. Takatsuki is notably absent from this dream that she shares with him, pointing to his actual insignificance in her life; he is only one of many sex objects she uses for creativity’s sake. The girl masturbates in the boy’s bed, further removing Takatsuki from his role of sexual partner. Takatsuki has reason to envy Kafuku; Oto never had any love for him.

The relationship to one’s parents is one of endless submission. I write this in the months following the regular deaths of both grandfathers, over whom neither of my parents ever held the upper hand. Even now my father, despite perpetual disaffection, contends with feelings he could only ever put on hold. I am sure to do the same. Festen platforms the attempts of four children to revenge themselves upon their parents, a universal desire. They get closer than most: embarrassing, beating, and ultimately denying him their presence. But even for protagonist Christian, who succeeds in humiliating his father and uniting his family against him, there is nothing he can do to reverse his abuse. What does Christian gain from the night of revenge? Momentary satisfaction. What does Christian suffer? He suffers betrayal from his brother and mother, abandonment by his living sister, humiliations of his own. In the morning, spirits cooled, Helge gives a genuinely apologetic speech that none of his

children interrupt. Though he is ushered upstairs, he retains the last word, the right to solicit forgiveness. After all is said, they are still his children, they still bear the weight of family history and heredity.

Never before has such an otherwise good album been so entrenched in pop culture ephemera. The lyrics categorically suck, and the singing really taints the rest of the album because it’s mixed so high; every purely instrumental second is superior to whenever Mr. Quaverer opens his little mouth. The nontraditional rock instruments define the album to me, since they’re what differentiate it from all of its equally guitar-conscious peers. The violin rocks every second it’s featured but isn’t really a major feature, and while the saxophone adds a twist on the music that perks my ears up, often it sputters reedily and makes me wonder if literally any other timbre would fit better. Though the sound on this album is arguably unique, it sounds to me more like a new collage of common and poorly executed sounds. The atonal guitar in “Science Fair” doesn’t sound explosive like its punk forefathers, it sounds sloppy. The opening to “Athens, France” is aping the band the pop culture poet namedrops the following track. The sudden turn halfway through “Sunglasses” is surprising, but mostly disappointing considering how much worse the second part is than the first. “Opus” is the best track and one I can see myself returning to. That song actually feels like a united effort from all of the musicians rather than just a quilt of ideas. The lyrics don’t turn me off, and there’s a great buildup throughout the song. It’s really great all around, and I hope future releases from the band follow in its footsteps.

title: Funeral
creator: Arcade Fire
review: From the first track, Funeral demands something from its listeners that we are not yet able to give: vulnerability. The opening track and all subsequent assume a camaraderie with the listener, sharing deep feelings and lamentations about childhood. An album must convince a listener that it's emotional content is worthwhile, but Funeral brazenly assumes it. The instrumental content is not strong enough to carry the touchy-feely motions, in fact, the instrumental content adds to the violation of emotional boundaries: orchestral strings and a cavernous sound production channels classical music, which is known for its ability to tug at one's heartstrings with just a crescendo. But classical itself relies on build-up to grab an audience. Almost every song on this album begins and ends with the same musical phrases or sections, thus achieving no progress. Compare Funeral to it's thematic peer of the same year, The Polyphonic Spree’s Together We’re Heavy. This album changes, moves, and deserves an audience’s vulnerability in the way Funeral doesn't. The positive aspects of Funeral include the fact that many of the instruments are used well and at opportune times; despite my belief that they don't achieve their purpose of deepening an audience's emotional tether to this album, the instruments are still powerful. They elevate the songs above simple pop, giving depth to harmonies and creating a cohesive sound to the album. Furthermore, the themes of childhood trust, and of course, community (see Neighbourhood #1-4) are established through lyrics and bolstered by bittersweet melodies.

title: Illmatic
creator: Nas
review: As Nas’ magnum opus, Illmatic stands the test of time that many rap albums of the early nineties don't, whether hindered by poor production or woefully dated references. The first track hits you with a sound that is New York, and the rest of the album follows suit. One of Illmatic’s more subtle qualities is its use of features. Only two of the ten songs include other artists, just enough to maintain listener interest. The features themselves are woven in perfectly: they take up the choruses, so that Nas can pick up slack in the verses, where he shines. Q-tip gives a better performance in One Love than in his entire career with A Tribe Called Quest. This album’s beats and backing instrumentals are strong; each track has something unique, such as the record scratching on The World is Yours or the xylophone on One Love. This album is carefully put together: no part of it is innovative, but all of it is well organised. “Nasty” Nas’ skill lies in his eye for control. His verses are deft, changing pace and slipping internal rhymes at every available opportunity yet maintaining order. This is contrasted against his choruses. They have little more than one or two lines, and they are repeated exhaustively, to the point of assimilation within the beat. The lyrical content itself is strong, giving us insight into life in New York City’s rougher patches. Illmatic’s strength is clearly in its polish. It is rough enough to sound authentically East Coast, but refined in the way that Nas’ peers could not achieve without sounding diluted. It fails in innovation, however. Rap has been around for decades by Nas’ arrival to the scene, and has proved itself to be less than versatile. Nas is good, but conventional.

title: Le deuxième sexe [The Second Sex]
creator: Simone de Beauvoir
review: Despite containing many inaccuracies, The Second Sex is widely regarded as the most seminal work in feminist literature. Its size and breadth of subject matter lend credence to this title, but its faults should not be ignored. De Beauvoir is not a biologist, but she makes a number of biological claims that are often speculative (such as her continued reference to hermaphrodites despite their near-nonexistence) or plainly wrong (for instance, her statement that more women than men die between the ages of fourteen and twenty-two, which is a statistical falsehood that has never been true of the general population. These inaccuracies detract from her credibility in every topic but philosophy, which requires no concrete evidence or facts, things de Beauvoir obviously struggles with. Furthermore, it seems at times that de Beauvoir uses meaningless statements to pad her book, such as “The tremendous advance accomplished by psychoanalysis over psychophysiology…” These koans bring confusion and distract from her main points. Her entire chapter of psychoanalysis is based on Freud, who is not nearly as respected now as he was then. The chapters on history are especially troublesome. With no footnotes to speak of, it no longer becomes a matter of refutation to disagree with de Beauvoir, but rather simple dismission, as the burden is on de Beauvoir to prove her claims, not the reader to believe her. Considering the size of her assertions, most of her book must be considered bunk for any purpose besides stimulating the imagination. De Beauvoir makes some valid and interesting claims, such as the idea that men are instilled with an autonomy early on that women are not by way of their urinary function, in that men can manipulate their penis and therefore master their urination, whereas women are more inclined to feel submissive to their bodily function. These insightful ideas are however overshadowed by a lack of evidence and the breadth of incorrect information present in the book.

review: Much like its spiritual predecessor Incredibles, Megamind introduces the concept of trope deconstruction to children in a well-conceived and understandable manner, preserving a compelling plot along with its demonstrated themes and humour. Unfortunately, Megamind does not commit fully to the deconstruction; a mistake most obvious in Tina Fey’s character of Roxanne Ritchie who is a complete helpless damsel in distress. The ending also disappoints, with a musical number that accompanies a montage of all loose ends being cleaned up, which commits the cardinal sin of being a tired trope and kitschy. There are a collection of other tropes this film falls victim to, such as the in media res flash forward opening that the film returns to at the end or The greatest plot issue in this film is due in that much of the character development (most notably Ritchie’s swift development from hating to appreciating Megamind) feels rushed. This is in large part due to the ambition of the film seeking large, believable twists, subversions, and moral messages. If given more time and care, these character developments could become more believable. This would, of course, require a longer film, ultimately alienating it from its intended audience.

title: Зеркало [Mirror]

review: Confusing, clearly some sort of koan. Hard to keep track of the names, but that's Russian for ya. Always feels like you're on the verge of getting a clue, but it never arrives. Don’t confuse it for a surrealist piece á la Altman or Lynch; I don’t believe the essence of this film is transmitted through an emotional undercurrent caused by dreamlike passages. I think there is a conscious logic, or illogic, to the film, with wildly different scenes following each other to create distinct meaning. I don’t think this meaning is objective, the film is clearly open to many different interpretations, but I do think the film aims to create a puzzling narrative that can be consciously understood. It is not merely a set of scenes that must be understood unconsciously, as with a surrealism.

The density of jokes that Monty Python is known for is not present in this film, which is a major fault as a high quantity of jokes serves as quality assurance: failed jokes are forgotten as new jokes are presented. The story itself isn't very strong either. The irreverence of the film's nature doesn't excite as much as it prevents sticking to a strong plot line.

title: Necessary Illusions
creator: Noam Chomsky
review: What a letdown following Manufacturing Consent. This book is no more than a weak addendum to that masterpiece. Where the Herman-Chomsky opus has concise examples, clear argument, and engaging structure, Necessary Illusions has examples that go on too long without reaching a defined point, a stagnant and vague thesis of “media serves power”, and is mystifyingly structured into a short text followed by a series of plotless appendices. This book could be simply formulated as a comparison of the case studies of US media treatment of Nicaragua and Israel. That’s all this book is. Instead, Chomsky flits between the two studies without rhyme or reason, alternating information about the case studies in nonsensical sequence.

title: Nightcrawler
creator: Dan Gilroy
review: A solid film idea with mediocre execution that could have benefited from an extra hour of characterisation and slower escalation to a more meaningful climax rather than the one-dimensional characters and rushed ending offered. The film's best qualities are Gyllenhaal’s acting and the satire of neoliberalism, with most of his lines being truisms such as “If you want to win the lottery, you have to work to make the money to buy a ticket” and “Do you know what fear stands for? False Evidence Appearing Real”, and rehearsed, work-fetishising lines such as “I know that today’s work culture no longer caters to the job loyalty that could be promised to earlier generations”, etc., but played to the extreme in an antisocial character. This is the best part of the film and should have been its focus. Nightcrawler mirrors a similar black comedy, American Psycho, in both its critique of high-level capitalism and failure to commit to its own excellent concept. Also clear is its directorial debt to Martin Scorsese films, especially Taxi Driver, with dragging shots of Gyllenhaal’s blank face in the car and the overwrought mirror scene.

I agreed to this album because I made her listen to Metallica’s Ride the Lightning with me on a train and I owed her. The cuteness and sincerity of Pretty. Odd. broke through my makeshift elitism and I danced with my girlfriend for a while to this record, adding it to my streaming library soon after. It's far from perfect; relying partially on nostalgia, and possessing a large number of “fly-over” tracks, especially in the back half. No song on the album benefits from close listening, since the singing is the only real attraction. But what singing! And for every song that disappoints whenever you pay attention, there's a different song that is so refreshingly earnest that you don't care enough to think hard about it.

The guitarwork is fantastic in its own right, more complex than is traditional of folk music. Has the power to get one in touch with their more shameful feelings of resentment and hopelessness. title: Rushmore
creator: Wes Anderson
review:
Never before have I been so conflicted about a film. On the one hand, I have a longstanding aesthetic predilection for homosociality, which this film explores with beautiful style and a veneer of innocence, such that the audience may discover friendship all over again. Furthermore, while I do not have so strong a fascination with boarding schools, I do have deep personal experience with them and this element of the film pulls at my heartstrings in a more personal way. So from a critical distance I can enjoy the core relationship of the film and appreciate the auteur cinematography, while I have a personal relationship with the setting. For all the faults that I will soon get to, the style is really a high point, as it is in all of Anderson’s films. Each room is like a model house with its nonverbal exploration of its denizen’s character. The setting speaks more than the characters do! But there is much that disappoints. For one, every single needle-drop is jarring and inappropriate. I have an appreciation for the tenets of the Dogme 95, but I am not an ideologue who opposes all

non-diegetic sound. The use of music in this film is simply amateurish: there are far too many songs, they overlay montages that deserve to actually be explored, the songs do not fit their scenes, and the songs themselves are generally poor. Additionally, we have a terrible mix of flat characters acting out a meandering plot. Ms. Cross is merely a means to an end: a loosely attractive young woman over whom our two protagonists may pine. Herman Blume wanders directionless through this movie, lost whenever he is unattached to Max, who himself is driven, but an empty vessel. We get glimpses of pathos: Max obscures his father’s profession out of shame, Blume betrays his friend for the woman. Just as often, however, we have unbelievable character beats like Blume’s abuse at the hands of his sons and Max’s easily resolved spats. Not much happens in this film that advances the characters’ goals or plot, but there are plenty of films where nothing important happens and there are no rules about what a plot should be. It is disappointing, however, when one is sitting and watching a story that continually proves there is no reason to believe an arc will resolve, one may be frustrated that the characters acting out this story are equally unattached to its outcome, merely wooden automatons that act it out. It would be Beckettian if it wasn’t so damn twee.

A psychoanalysis applied to all humanity, this work reveals little about its subject due to reliance on bunk science, but a humanity’s worth about Paglia herself.

title: 渋星 [Shibuboshi]
creator: 渋さ知らズ [Shibusashirazu]
review: Really exciting jazz fusion that shows the potential for experimentation in a genre that has floundered since Miles Davis left the scene. The songs are explosive and dense, with enough instruments that I’ve spent several listens noticing something I missed previously. This is such a huge improvement from the bands amateurish debut, now a classic in the genre and one of the best jazz albums of the 21st century. I wish the drums were a bit quieter, since next to the bass they’re the least impressive instrument. Why does it seem that every recent jazz album has questionable mixing? Maybe I’m too used to Teo Macero and Bob Thiele’s ’70s style, but it seems modern producers lack the ear for balance, which is so important in big band albums like this. It is difficult to make an album this instrumentally dense emotive. A suite of instruments can get bogged down in the myriad virtuosity of the musicians. In Shibuboshi, though, each instrument is working together to produce exciting songs that never feel too technical. Shibuboshi is a great album because it’s not just a collection of isolated musicians playing together, nor is it a monolithic ensemble wall of sound. It’s an orchestral experience, carrying on where American jazz musicians like Miles Davis and John McLaughlin left off in their foray into rock.

review: One cannot review Team Sleep’s work without viewing it in context of its more famous and popular sibling, Deftones. Team Sleep, the band's sole release, is a self-titled album released the same year Deftones released their own self-titled album, the one that heralded the decline of their career. Team Sleep features elements Deftones is known for (precise drums, wailing vocals, dark atmosphere) with a softer touch, best exemplified by vocalist Chino Moreno limiting the Mountain Dew flavoured shouts and growls he is known for and the quieter, cleaner guitars. The album is also pretty electronic; you have Death Grips’ Zach Hill to thank for that (Chino Moreno and Zach Hill on this album and they managed to not make nü metal?). Although an excellent album, Team Sleep does not impress in every regard: it is still just an indie rock album. It is in some ways outdone by its Deftones predecessor, White Pony, which is more experimental and features better instrumental work. Team Sleep does not keep you interested throughout the entire album; there are some boring tracks that feel too conventional to deserve attention. Team Sleep plays like an emotionally vulnerable White Pony with more electronic elements that still manages to find its own voice.

title: The Black Parade
creator: My Chemical Romance
review: Pop-punk that's gotten a bit too big for its britches, and, frankly, a bit too pop. The best parts of this album are the echoes of the previous record, mostly Gerard Way’s singing and occasional growling. The pretentious attempts at orchestral emo definitely detract from the album’s verisimilitude. I have to admit that my enjoyment of this album is couched in my longest high school relationship; while her introduction of Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge changed my mind about pop punk and kneecapped my paternally inherited music elitism, I did not care at all for The Black Parade at the time, for which the first paragraph of this review, written when I was about 17, yields testimony. This album was always her favourite, though, and it is the more nostalgic of the two because of how her theatricality and lugubriousness matched this record that I was so excited to tell her did not count as “real emo” as soon as I heard American Football for the first time. The better of the two pop-punk rock operas of the period, garrotting American Idiot, its songs actually hit if one checks their cynicism at the door. The root of scepticism around pop punk and dark cabaret lies in the feeling that it is deeply disingenuous. We want our music to feel real, to contain some truth that only art can convey. When art seems to lie, like middle-class Tom Waits putting on a scoundrel rasp, the authenticity-concerned among us close themselves off to the truth that can pass through when one dispenses with whatever cynicism can comfortably be shed. The aesthetic truth of art lies not in the art itself, but in our appreciation of it. Barthes’ 1967 essay applies to all art. This album made me cringe when it felt like a histrionic lament to which only self-pitying tweens magnifying their own microtraumas could relate. But it helped my girlfriend at that time, who certainly had real problems. If this album was true to her, may not artists who lie indeed speak truths through their art? The demand for authenticity in art may be merely a failure in the imaginative capacity of troubled listeners.

title: The Logic of Capital: An Introduction to Marxist Economic Theory
creator: Deepankar Basu
review: The economic thought of Karl Marx deserves to be taken seriously. Indeed, he may be one of history’s greatest thinkers on economics, even if most of his ideas, like the labour theory of value, have not stood the test of time. Deepankar Basu, a heterodox economist at the heterodox UMass Amherst Department of Economics, does an excellent job of extending Marx’s thought to modern methods with a minimum of deviation. This is an impressive feat because Marx wrote prior to essential conceptual/mathematical developments in economics such as the marginal revolution and development of econometric methods. Most who try to extend Marx to modern methods must make extreme alterations to Marx’s thought in order to maintain logical consistency, such as the analytical Marxists who dispensed with key features like dialectics and the aforementioned labour theory of value. This work remains as close to Marx’s thought as possible while adapting to advanced methods and developments, which is both its strength and its weakness. It is the best defense of Marxian economics that I have read, but its failure to convince me has led me to move on from orthodox Marxism as a workable framework.

title: The Loser
creator: Gospel
review:
Nearly two decades since their last and only other album, and the wait was worth its vintage. Even more than its cousins in emo and extreme metal, screamo has been snubbed as low-brow, immature. Is there any album that better threatens that narrative? The Loser’s progressive instrumentation refracts the genre’s eponymous singing style, often too raw to communicate any nuance, into new emotional territories that are harder to pin down than words. This album’s emotional palette is too esoteric for me to describe. To me, the joy of music consists in discovering new aesthetic-emotional experiences, and by that metric The Loser is this year’s greatest success. The only real issue with this album is one I have found with many progressive records of the past few years: the peculiar instrumentation and particularised emotions necessary to make music unique preclude the formation of a gestalt. The album is merely a collection of excellent songs, as cohesion belongs to the music of broader emotional strokes.

06/08/2026: Given some time, my appreciation for this album has mellowed.

It doesn’t meander quite like it used to, but it has the quality of sounding like a pop song not realising that its singer just finished her last verse. He has to start singing to stop, though; the most unique facet of this band’s songs is the way that most songs carry on longer than you would expect them to last. Unfortunately this album is the dying breath of all this band’s unique qualities, so enjoy the few occasions of wandering basslines and exploding guitar riffs when they occasionally show up over the album’s runtime.

The previous, gloomy Bend Sinister, had been released seventeen years prior, when avant-punk was long out of style and the Fall were the last of the punk collagists; gone were the Velvet Underground, Swell Maps, This Heat. By 2003, little had changed. The only notable avant-punk release had been 1994’s Strangers From the Universe, which met no recognition. Of course, the Fall had kept making music all this time. How could they not? Mark E. Smith’s creative output wasn’t something that stopped, slowed, or abated. Unlike other artists, like Bowie, who also went through a long drought of duds preceding a late-period masterpiece, Smith had not been running on empty until rediscovering his creative libido. In every Fall album, even the bad ones, there is a unique creative force, it just doesn’t always manage to recognise its own ambition. Smith and the Fall had been making The Real New Fall LP for seventeen years. Its subtitle, Formerly Country on the Click might as well say Formerly Cerebral Caustic, formerly Middle Class Revolt, formerly the Infotainment Scan, formerly... Finally, Smith’s creative efforts bore a complete fruit. A postmodern pastiche of influences that are recognisable as such but unidentifiable on their own. The shape of punk that went.

title: This Is a Long Drive for Someone with Nothing to Think About

review: As the title suggests, this album evokes feelings of a long, empty journey. It rewards aimless, brainless wandering, which is not meant pejoratively. Isaac Brock sings of losing battles with oneself and one’s environment; the lyrics are a blue collar cry for help through an abrasive voice that almost seems to tear in despair at points. The guitar on this album, however, is the centerpiece. Stretches of solos can fill songs, and even extend beyond them when turns the music off. That is the power of this album: the feeling of stretching highways and endless travel create an oppressive environment reminiscent of Mekons’ Fear and Whiskey. Not much can be said for the bass, because it seamlessly glues songs together, giving a rhythm to the assault of Brock’s cracking vocals and screeching guitar. Jeremiah Green’s drums mirror the guitarwork, assaulting the hi-hat during “Tundra/Desert” or playing short rhythmic phrases during tracks like “Ohio”. Of course, the Green’s drumming makes itself truly unique in the way that it deviates from its own patterns to introduce guitar phrases or play slower to defer attention to the lyricism. The best term for his style of playing is “cooperative”, a welcome quality of a wholly uncooperative album.

Punchy, fun drums combine with surprisingly interesting guitarwork. The vocals themselves have actual substance, blending melody with abrasive growls and squawks. This album has actual emotional depth that, despite having little self-awareness as was common for its contemporaries, cannot simply be written off as sophomoric whining. It is not, however, perfect. The lyrical content is needlessly histrionic at many points in this album. Furthermore, although the guitarwork and drumming are the highlights of this album, they too can be predictable. My other main criticisms are of the inability of the album to innovate much, the lack of ambition for this album, which could have achieved more sonically, and the poor bass guitar.

title: Vortex Temporum
creator: Gérard Grisey
review: Perhaps I lose some of the enjoyment of this composition because of my completely amateur knowledge of spectral technique. I know little about the technical aspect of this specific piece, my familiarity is limited to spectralism as a whole, and it would take a great deal of reading to familiarise myself with the theoretical basis of Vortex Temporum in particular. I think the only two qualities of music I recognise are aesthetic quality and originality. With rock music and some jazz I can decompose music to theory with some success, although it is not apparent to me that this is an important quality of music for the listener. It seems more likely to me that theory should be important only to the composer and the audience should solely care about their listening pleasure. There may be something to be said for the improvement of listening pleasure from better knowledge of musical theory. In any case, the spectral method is complex enough that dissertations are written about it, and some of Vortex Temporum’s intended effect is lost on me. What sounds avant-garde to me must be purely academic to the composer. From an aesthetic perspective: put off most by the piano solo that makes up most of the first movement, somewhat bored and reminded of Glenn Branca (who no doubt bears a great debt to early spectralists) in the second, and most taken with the final movement, especially the strings and woodwinds.
